understand.concept: Type annotations document the values a function or variable is intended to use. They help readers, IDEs and static type checkers reason about a program, but Python does not automatically enforce ordinary annotations at runtime. Use `str | None` for an optional string and `int | str` for a value that may have either type. Validate untrusted runtime data separately.
understand.whyItMatters: Clear contracts make larger applications easier to understand and maintain without pretending annotations replace runtime validation.
understand.analogy: Annotations are labels on storage containers that tell a team what belongs there.
understand.analogyLimit: A label does not stop someone from placing the wrong object in the container; runtime checks and validation are separate.
understand.summary: Type Annotations, Optional Values and Union Types develops practical application engineering skills for Python projects.

explain.narrative:
## Annotate contracts, then validate data
Use built-in types such as `str`, `int`, `list[str]` and unions such as `str | None` (Python 3.10+). Annotate parameters and return values to communicate intent. A static type checker can report incompatible calls before execution, but the interpreter normally does not reject a value just because it conflicts with an annotation. At external boundaries, parse and validate actual values. Prefer precise types over `Any`, and keep annotations aligned with implementation.
